library(ALA)

data(fev1)

fev1_df <- filter(fev1, age > 10, age < 11) %>%

```{r 4.3_calcs}

# Caculating as a proportional fraction of the data set
summarise(fev1_df ,
          `FEV1> 2.5` = mean(FEV1 > 2.5),
          `1.5 <FEV1< 2.5` = mean(FEV1 < 2.5 & FEV1 >  1.5))


# Expected from a normal model
pnorm(2.5,
      mean = mean(fev1_df$FEV1),
      sd = sd(fev1_df$FEV1),
      lower.tail = FALSE)



pnorm(2.5,
                mean = mean(fev1_df$FEV1),
                sd = sd(fev1_df$FEV1)) -
     pnorm(1.5,
               mean = mean(fev1_df$FEV1),
               sd = sd(fev1_df$FEV1))



```
The results we get from the data are similar to, but not the same as, the model. The model is a function describing population. The sampled data are used to obtain model parameters.



```{r Quantile_calcs}

quantile(x = fev1_df$FEV1, seq(0,1,by=0.25))




```


The corresponding quantiles of our normal model are:

## 0% 25% 50% 75% 100%
# -Inf 1.698 1.91 2.123 Inf

The endpoints are infinite because 0% of real numbers are less than -∞ and 100% of real numbers are less than ∞.

IT IS A MODEL, NOT THE SAMPLE OR POPULATION



Last module we introduced the concept of the standard normal distribution: Z~N(0,1). We transform a random variable X ~N(μ, σ^2) by

1) subtracting μ
2)dividing by σ.

While the histograms we’ve seen are one way of visually assessing the fit of a normal distribution, we can plot the quantiles of the data against the hypothesised quantiles to check the distribution fit. This allows us to visually assess whether a set of observations is normal with **stat_qq() from ggplot2**. We need to pass in standardised values, so the variable has a mean zero and a standard deviation of one.

We compare whether quantiles of standardised values match quantiles of
. If the quantiles are similar, then X may be normal.


*What the quantile quantile plot does is compute the slope and intercept of the line connecting the points at specified quartiles of the theoretical and sample distributions*


```{r}
library(ALA)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
data(fev1)

fev1_df <- filter(fev1, age > 10, age < 11) %>%
     mutate(FEV1 = exp(logFEV1)) %>%
     group_by(id) %>%
     filter(row_number() == 1) %>% ungroup()


# Standardised dataset - normalisation?
fev1_df <-mutate(fev1_df,
           FEV.std = (FEV1 - mean(FEV1))/sd(FEV1))

# Graph it
fev1_dfqq <- ggplot(data=fev1_df, aes(sample=FEV.std))+
     stat_qq(alpha=0.1, geom="point", pch=16)+
     coord_equal()+
     geom_abline()+
     theme_bw()+
     xlab("Z ~ N(0,1)")+
     ylab(expression(Standardised~FEV[1]))

fev1_dfqq


```
Here we see that apart from the two extreme positive values (really big FEV1) there’s good agreement. We can say that our assumption of normally distributed data holds.



# 4.5 The likelihood function

Likelihood takes the opposite approach, it asks the question: 'What kind of population could have created my data?'. That is, what parameters could have produced my data?


Parametric probability model f_i can be the same of different for each i theta is a parameter for all PMFs or PDFs
\( X_i \sim f_i(x;\theta)\)

Likelihood function 
\(L(\Theta) = \prod^n_{i=1} f(X_i ; \Theta)\)


Note: (\(\prod\)) is the product of the series

This needs calculus to maximise, I haven't copied this function as it is seems crazy.

The Maximum Likelihood Estimator is denoted \(\hat{\theta}_{MLE}\). The true parameter is \(\theta\).


# Parameter Uncertainty

We estimated the population mean, μ, with sample mean \(\bar{X}\). 
We estimated the population standard deviation, σ, with the sample standard deviation s.

If we take a different sample we will very likely get a different sample mean and sample s


The variability in \(\bar{X}\)  is due to the variability in X. 

*The standard error of the mean is:*

\(se_{\overline{x}}=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\)

The standard error of the mean is heavily dependent on sample size.

As we collect more data, the sample mean looks more like the population mean. Over many simulations, the mean is normally distributed and is our derived statistic.

It’s often common to report an estimate of the mean as \(\overline{x}±se_\overline{x}\).

On its own this does not give us information on the value of the mean.

*Central Limit Theorem*

\(Z =\frac{\overline{x}-\mu{}}{\sigma{}/\sqrt{n}}\sim{}N\left(0,1\right)\)

Z score is measure of probability?


# T tests


We have p-values, rejection regions and test statistics to help us decide on the outcome of a test. Lecturer suggests only using one for a t test

_Rough Procedure:_

1) Specify a *null hypothesis(\(H_0\))*: states what we’d expect to see if there was no difference. 
2) Specify an *alternative hypothesis(\(H_1\) )*: describes an outcome that we’d describe as 'different'.
3) Formulate some test statistic from our data and hypotheses that describes how probable this result is if the null were true. 
4) We then consider whether we have evidence to reject the null hypothesis.


Let's consider the following example. The National Asthma Council guidelines (2006) specify that for 12-year-old boys, the normal (population mean) is 1.61. Our data has \(\frac{}{x} = 1.65\) and \(se_\overline{x} = 0.254\) . How close is this 1.65 to 1.61? We want to know if our group’s mean is lower than 1.61, indicating poor lung health. Our null hypothesis is that the sample mean is the same as the population. Our alternative hypothesis is  where it is less. In other words, the alternative is that the group’s mean is less than the guideline. 


If we knew the population statistics accurately we would be able to use the Z score from the central limit theorem for a normal distribuition. (Need to have done a full census)

If we only have sample statistics we need to use a student's t distribution and estimate a parameter like this:

\(Z=\frac{\overline{x}-{\mu{}}_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}=\frac{1.65-1.61}{0.254/\sqrt{7}}=0.416\)


We want to find the probability to the left of 0.416 in a t(6) (v= 6 degrees of freedom):


```{r}
x <- c(1.61, 1.65, 1.45, 1.36,
2.12, 1.82, 1.54)
xbar <- mean(x)
(ts <- (xbar - 1.61)/(sd(x)/sqrt(length(x))))
## [1] 0.4163828
(p <- pt(q=ts, lower.tail = TRUE, df = 6))
## [1] 0.6541928

#Lets see what that looks like:

library(ggplot2)
ggplot()+
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, # plot a rormal
    args = list(mean=0,sd = 1),
    aes(xmin=-4,
          xmax=4,
          ymin =0,
          ymax = ..y..))+
  stat_function(fun = dnorm,
    args = list(mean=0,sd=1),
    xlim=c(-4,ts),
    geom="area",
    fill="blue",
    alpha=0.25)+
  labs(x="x",y="y")+
  theme_bw()


```


The probability of observing something at least as extreme (in the left tail) as Z = 0.4163828 is 0.6541928. This is called the p value

For any null hypothesis-based test that produces a test statistic, the p value is the answer to the question 'what is the *probability* of observing a test statistic at least as big as this if the null hypothesis were actually true?'


The p value is not the probability that our result is due to chance. **If p<α we have evidence to reject \(H_0\). The value doesn’t tell us we have evidence to accept \(H_1\) ** 

**This seems to be a very important point as is is often misused apparently**

With α=0.05 we would reject \(H_0:μ=1.61\) if p value <0.05. Our value is 0.6541928, which means we don’t have evidence against \(H_0\). As far as we can tell, this group’s mean is at the guideline.


**Confidence intervals**

To construct a confidence interval for our mean, we must choose a level of statistical significance, α, such that  \((1-α)×100\)
is the confidence level we wish to use. For example, a 95% confidence interval corresponds to α = 0.05.



We can use t.test in R instead of calculating the long way:

```{r}

x <- c(1.61, 1.65, 1.45, 1.36, 2.12, 1.82, 1.54)

t.test(x=x, alternative="less", mu=1.61)


```
# 4.9 Case Study

In this activity, we will be investigating the uncertainty in our estimate of the mean age of death in Brisbane Hospital from 1899 to 1913. We will be using the Deaths (CSV 112KB) Download Deaths (CSV 112KB) data file.


```{r}
setwd("D:/Morgan/Downloads")
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
deaths_df<-read_csv("deaths.csv")



```
We will asssume:

\(X∼N(μ,σ^2)\) or that X is similar to a normal distribution so that we can estimate population statistics from our sample ones.

```{r}

death_summary <- summarise(deaths_df,
                           xbar = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE),
                           s = sd(Age, na.rm = TRUE),
                           n = n())%>%
  mutate(SE_xbar = s/n^0.5) # Can also use the function std.error()
  



ggplot(deaths_df, aes(x = Age))+
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = 'lightblue', colour = 'darkgrey',
                 aes(y = ..density..))+ # This line might be needed to get stat function to work?
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, # plot a normal
                args =list(mean = death_summary$xbar, # with mean xbar
                sd = death_summary$s))+ # and standard deviations
  theme_bw()



```
Now do a quantile-quantile plot to evaluate how normal it s

```{r}

df_stand_deaths <- mutate(deaths_df,
                          Age.std = (Age - mean(deaths_df$Age, na.rm = T))/
               sd(deaths_df$Age, na.rm = T))

ggplot(data= df_stand_deaths, aes(sample=Age.std)) +
     stat_qq(alpha= 0.5 , geom="point", pch=16) +
     coord_equal() +
     geom_abline() +
     theme_bw() +
     xlab("Z ~ N(0,1)") +
     ylab("Standardised Age")

```

The confidence interval for our mean population age of death (during the years 1899 to 1913), μ, is given by:

\(\overline{x}+t_{\alpha{}/2}(\nu{})\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}<\mu{}<\overline{x}+t_{1-\alpha{}/2}(\nu{})\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\)

in this case v = n-1, where we had n observations but have to estimate one parameter s to calculate our standard error. If we knew what the population standard deviation was σ we would not lose one degree of freedom.


*Use the following to calulate the confidence interval for  \(\alpha = 0.05\)*

```{r}
options(pillar.sigfig = 3)

#qt is the quantile function for a students t distribuition (which is standardised)

ci_95 <- mutate(death_summary, 
                q2.5 = qt(p = 0.025, df = n - 1),
                q97.5 = qt(p = 0.975, df = n - 1),
                L = xbar + q2.5 * s,
                U = xbar + q97.5 * s
                )



```
